title: Soloist or crowd? Topologies and the multi-agent bill
brief: One agent is struggling, and someone proposes a team of agents. The coupling of the subtasks, the value per run, the trust boundaries and the latency budget are all undecided. Compare the topologies against the evidence before you split anything.

blocks.text: Five ways to share the work, and what the evidence says

blocks.title: Multi-agent topologies
blocks.intro: Microsoft lists sequential, concurrent, group chat (including maker-checker loops), handoff and magentic orchestration [[r9]]. LangChain frames the same space as subagents, handoffs, skills, router and custom workflow [[r32]]. The key question is who owns the conversation after a delegation.

options.name: Supervisor with agents as tools
options.summary: A primary agent calls specialists like functions, keeps ownership and receives control back with each result.
pros: The caller stays accountable for the final answer
Workers can be read-only and hold least-privilege tools
cons: Every hop passes through the supervisor
The supervisor's window collects every result
options.bestWhen: One agent must own the answer and combine several specialist results.
options.avoidWhen: A specialist should talk to the user directly for the rest of the conversation.

options.name: Handoff mesh
options.summary: No central orchestrator: the receiving agent takes full ownership and the full context. In the OpenAI Agents SDK a handoff is exposed as a tool named transfer_to_<agent_name> by default [[r20]].
pros: The right specialist talks to the user with no return hop
Each specialist owns its tools, policy and owner
cons: Infinite handoff loops and bouncing are a documented risk [[r9]]
Microsoft's handoff supports Agent only, and agents must support local tool execution [[r11]]
options.bestWhen: Specialists should take over and own the rest of the conversation.
options.avoidWhen: The caller must combine several answers or stay accountable.

options.name: Group chat and maker-checker
options.summary: Several agents take turns in a shared conversation, often one produces and another reviews.
pros: Review loops raise quality when criteria are clear
cons: Stalls and non-terminating chats need a stop rule
options.bestWhen: A produce-and-review loop has a clear acceptance check.
options.avoidWhen: The path is deterministic or latency is tight.

options.name: Magentic
options.summary: A manager keeps shared context and a task ledger, tracks progress and re-plans. Built on the Magentic-One design [[r31]].
pros: A visible, adjustable plan for open-ended work
cons: Microsoft says it is untested how well it performs outside the original Magentic-One design, and the C# types are experimental [[r10]]
options.bestWhen: Open-ended work where a plan ledger is worth the cost and the wait.
options.avoidWhen: The task is time-sensitive or the path is deterministic.

options.name: Sequential or concurrent pipeline
options.summary: Fixed stages of specialists in order, or independent perspectives run in parallel and merged.
options.bestWhen: The stages are known, or the perspectives are independent.
options.avoidWhen: What one stage finds should change the later stages.

blocks.title: Single agent, or which crowd?
blocks.prompt: Flip the dials. Parallel writers are not on the board because no setting rescues them.

options.name: Single agent with tools
options.summary: One loop, one window, one decision maker.

options.name: Orchestrator with read-only workers
options.summary: Lead delegates reads and keeps the pen.

options.summary: Agents take turns, often producer and reviewer.

reads.why: One agent can read many sources in sequence.

writes.why: One decision maker keeps writes consistent.

high.why: Leaves breadth and parallelism unused when value justifies the spend.

split.why: One identity and tool set spans zones that should stay separate.

slow.why: Fine, but long runs fill one window.

writes.why: Parallel workers writing one artifact is the failure Cognition describes. Keep one writer.

low.why: About 15x chat tokens is hard to repay on low-value runs.

high.why: Breadth-first work repaid the cost in Anthropic's research eval.

split.why: Workers can hold separate identities and tools.

fast.why: Parallel reads help, but planning and synthesis add calls.

writes.why: Ownership moves, so context and decisions must travel with it.

low.why: Cost depends on how often agents hand off.

split.why: Each specialist can own its tools, policy and owner.

fast.why: The specialist answers the user directly, with no return hop.

writes.why: A checker can review while one agent writes.

high.why: Review loops can lift quality when criteria are clear.

split.why: A shared thread exposes every message to every agent.

reads.why: A task ledger tracks open-ended gathering.

high.why: A plan ledger pays only on open-ended, high-value work.

fast.why: Microsoft advises against it for time-sensitive work.

blocks.takeaway: The single agent wins whenever writes are coupled and value is modest. Splitting needs a dial you can name: independent reads with high value, or a trust boundary.

items.symptom: Two workers edit the same artifact and the result contradicts itself
items.cause: Parallel writers make implicit decisions without seeing each other's actions (Cognition, 2025-06-12) [[r3]]
items.fix: Single-threaded writes. Workers read and report, one agent writes, and traces are shared in full, not only summaries.

items.symptom: Requests bounce between specialists, or a group chat never ends
items.cause: Handoff loops or no termination rule. MAST files unawareness of termination conditions and step repetition under system design issues [[r5]]
items.fix: Hop cap, handoff allow-list and a termination condition owned by the orchestrator.

items.symptom: The run reports success and the output fails a spot check
items.cause: No agent verified the result, a task verification failure [[r5]]
items.fix: An independent checker with a clean context and an external check such as tests or a schema.

items.symptom: Run time equals the slowest subagent every time
items.cause: Subagents ran synchronously, which Anthropic found created bottlenecks [[r2]]
items.fix: Run workers in parallel with timeouts and let the lead continue with partial results.

blocks.title: Anthropic and Cognition fit together
blocks.md: Anthropic's gain came from breadth-first research reads. Cognition argued on 2025-06-12 against parallel agents that write [[r3]]. On 2026-04-22 it said that view still holds for parallel-writer swarms, that several agents can contribute while writes stay single-threaded, and that a review loop works best when the reviewer shares no context with the coder. It reports Devin Review catching on average 2 bugs per pull request, about 58% severe (vendor-reported) [[r4]].

quiz.q: Which change in the situation flips the choice from a handoff to an agent-as-tool design?
options: The specialist should own the rest of the conversation and talk to the user directly in every later turn
The specialist needs the full conversation history to do its job
Handoffs are unavailable in the framework you picked
The caller must stay accountable for the final answer and combine several specialist results
quiz.explain: With agent-as-tool the primary agent keeps ownership and control returns to it, which is what accountability and result combination need. The first two describe reasons to hand off, and a handoff already passes the full context. Framework availability is a constraint, not a dial that changes the design.

quiz.q: Select every signal that justifies splitting one agent into several.
options: The prompt has grown many if-then-else branches that are hard to maintain
Tool selection keeps failing after you clarified the tool descriptions
Parts of the work must run under different identities, teams or trust zones
The single agent looked slow in one demo
A competitor announced a multi-agent product
quiz.explain: OpenAI advises maximizing a single agent first, then splitting when prompts hold many branches or tool selection fails after clearer descriptions. Separate trust boundaries can justify the extra cost on their own. One slow demo and a competitor's announcement are not engineering signals.

quiz.q: Match each topology to the failure it is most associated with.

pairs.r: Bouncing between agents in an infinite handoff loop
A conversation that stalls or never terminates
Planning and re-planning cost on work that did not need it
Conflicting implicit decisions in one shared artifact

quiz.explain: Each topology fails where its strength is overused: a mesh has no central stopper, a chat needs a stop rule, a planning manager spends tokens and time, and parallel writers cannot see each other's decisions.

quiz.q: A chat answer to a research question uses about 8,000 tokens. Using Anthropic's reported multiplier for multi-agent systems, roughly how many tokens would a multi-agent run on the same question use?
quiz.hint: Multi-agent systems used about 15x the tokens of chat.
quiz.explain: 8,000 x 15 = 120,000 tokens. The multiplier is vendor-reported on Anthropic's own research traffic, so treat it as an order of magnitude and measure your own. Using the 4x agent multiplier instead would give only 32,000.

takeaways: Ask who owns the conversation after a delegation: the caller (agent as tool) or the receiver (handoff).
Multi-agent systems used about 15x the tokens of chat in Anthropic's data, so they must be justified by value per run.
Reads parallelize safely, coupled writes do not. Keep a single writer and add read-only workers.
Handoff loops, stalled chats and unverified results are the named failures. Put hop caps, stop rules and an independent checker in the design.
